In June 1942, the most famous admiral in the US Navy was lying in a hospital bed in Pearl Harbor, covered in a skin disease so bad he couldn't sleep.

Bill Halsey was supposed to lead America's carriers into the biggest gamble of the Pacific War. Instead, he told Nimitz to give the job to Raymond Spruance.

Spruance was a cruiser admiral. Not a pilot. He had never commanded a carrier, never led an air battle, and now he was being handed two of the three flattops America had left in the Pacific, with Japan coming for Midway.

On the morning of June 4, he made the call that decided the war. Instead of waiting to close the distance, he launched nearly everything he had at long range, as early as he could, before the Japanese could hit him first. It was a huge risk. Planes would run low on fuel. Some never made it back.

By the end of the day, four Japanese carriers were burning. Akagi, Kaga, Soryu, Hiryu. Four of the six that attacked Pearl Harbor, gone in a single day.

Then came the part almost nobody talks about.

That night, every instinct said chase them. Finish it. But Spruance knew Yamamoto's battleships were out there, and in the dark his carriers would be sitting ducks against big guns. So he turned east and pulled back. Yamamoto was in fact steaming toward him hoping for a night fight. He never got it.

Spruance won the battle and then refused to lose it.

After Midway, Nimitz made him his chief of staff. The two men lived in the same quarters at Pearl and went on long walks together almost every day. Spruance was famous for those walks. Miles a day, rain or shine, thinking through the war.

Then Nimitz gave him the Fifth Fleet, and Spruance ran the Central Pacific drive. Tarawa. Kwajalein. Saipan. Iwo Jima. Okinawa.

Here's a detail most people don't know. The Navy used the same ships for two fleets. When Halsey was in command, it was Third Fleet. When Spruance took over, the exact same ships became Fifth Fleet. One admiral fought while the other planned the next campaign.

In June 1944 at the Philippine Sea, Japan threw its rebuilt carrier air force at him. American pilots shot down so many planes it got nicknamed the Great Marianas Turkey Shoot. Japanese naval aviation never recovered. Three more enemy carriers went to the bottom.

And he still got criticized. Aviators were furious he didn't charge west to chase the Japanese fleet. But his orders were to protect the Saipan landings, and he would not leave thousands of Marines exposed for a chance at glory.

Four months later at Leyte Gulf, Halsey did exactly what Spruance refused to do. He took the bait, chased a decoy force of Japanese carriers, and left an entire landing force nearly undefended. A handful of destroyers and escort carriers had to fight off Japanese battleships on their own.

Suddenly Spruance's caution didn't look so cautious anymore.

Off Okinawa in 1945, a kamikaze slammed into his flagship, USS Indianapolis. He moved to the battleship New Mexico. A few weeks later, kamikazes hit that one too. He kept commanding.

After the war, Congress had a limited number of five-star slots. Halsey got the fifth star. Spruance didn't. Congress later passed a law giving him full admiral's pay for life, which was basically an admission that he'd been shorted.

He never wrote a memoir. Never did the press tour. Never fought for his own legacy. He ran the Naval War College, served as ambassador to the Philippines, and went home.

When he died in 1969, he was buried at Golden Gate National Cemetery. Right next to him are Chester Nimitz, Kelly Turner, and Charles Lockwood. The four of them arranged it years earlier so they could rest together.

The quietest admiral of the war won its most important battle and then spent the rest of his life letting other people take the credit.

His name was Raymond Spruance. Remember it.
